final_message:
All done. All five versions are complete, verified, and benchmarked.

## Algorithm (identical in all five)

Single pass over the whole file in memory; no regex — a hand-written byte-level validator that mirrors the SPEC's regex exactly (fixed 25-byte timestamp prefix, `[a-z]+-\d+` server, exact method words, path segment scan, optional `?query`, 3-digit status, `\d+B` size, `\d+.\dms` latency, quoted UA that must end the line). While scanning the path it builds the template in a reusable scratch buffer (`/users/7/orders/` → `/users/{id}/orders/`), so no per-line string allocation. Per template it keeps a count and a growable array of latencies in tenths of a ms; status classes are 10 counters. At the end: sort templates by (count desc, template asc), take 10, sort each one's latencies, nearest-rank percentiles `ceil(p·n/100)`.

## Per-language speed choices

- **C++** (`cpp/main.cpp`): `fread` of whole file, pointer parsing, `memchr` line scan, `unordered_map` with C++20 heterogeneous lookup (`string_view` keys, allocation only on first sighting of a template), `to_chars` number formatting, single `fwrite`, binary stdout mode.
- **Java** (`java/src/Main.java`): `Files.readAllBytes`, SWAR (8-bytes-at-a-time) `\n` scan, `HashMap` with a reused mutable key object (content-equals/hashCode) so lookups allocate nothing; a copy is made only on first sighting. Latencies in `long[]`.
- **C#** (`csharp/Program.cs`): `File.ReadAllBytes`, `Span<byte>.IndexOf` (SIMD) line scan, `Dictionary` with the same mutable-key trick, ASCII output written to the raw standard-output stream (explicit `\n`, no `WriteLine` CRLF).
- **Go** (`go/main.go`): `os.ReadFile`, `bytes.IndexByte` (SIMD) line scan, `map[string]*agg` where the hot lookup `m[string(scratch)]` is the compiler's allocation-free conversion; a real copy is made only when inserting a new template.
- **JavaScript** (`js/main.js`): `readFileSync` Buffer, native `Buffer.indexOf(10)` line scan, byte-indexed parsing, and a custom open-addressing hash map (FNV-1a over a reusable `Uint8Array` scratch template, keys stored in a byte arena, aggregates in typed arrays) — zero per-line allocation; output built once and written in one `write`.

All five handle edge cases: empty file, missing trailing newline, malformed lines, 0xx–9xx classes, empty/huge queries, ties in the top-10, and saturate absurd (>10¹⁵ tenths) latencies instead of overflowing.

## Verification

A Python reference (`test/ref.py`, regex-based) was checked against all three provided samples, then used as ground truth. Each version passes:

| Input | cpp | java | csharp | go | js |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s1 (100 lines) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| s2 (2 000) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| s3 (100 000) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| big (2 000 000, 221 MB, ~1% malformed) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| edge cases (empty, no-trailing-\n, all-malformed, 15-template ties, 9xx, huge latencies) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Benchmark on the 2.21 MB… 221 MB / 2 M-line input (noisy shared machine, 4 runs)

| | C++ | Go | C# | JS (Node 22) | Java 23 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| time | **0.64–0.72 s** | 0.61–0.79 s | 0.97–1.17 s | 0.92–1.05 s | 1.05–1.40 s |
| peak memory | **~231 MB** | ~306 MB | ~283 MB | ~260 MB | ~530–830 MB |

C++ is both fastest and leanest (its memory ≈ the input buffer, which every version needs); Java carries the largest footprint and startup cost under default JVM flags (which `run.cmd` fixes — not changeable). Go/JS are close behind C++, C#/Java trade GC/runtime overhead for roughly 0.4–0.7 s more.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
